newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr climb pauses as altitude tells.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr climb pauses as altitude tells.

text.p: The Australian dollar lost a little lustre Monday as investors took profits on recent rich gains, but sentiment remained strongly bullish for the outlook.
Some consolidation was always on the cards after last week's lightening 2-1/2 cent advance and analysts reckoned a pullback could extend to US$0.8050/80 without troubling the uptrend.
Traders said U.S. funds and local exporters were keen to buy dips and more samurai-linked demand was expected, although a rumoured A$500 million issue had yet to make an appearance.
Domestic economic data showing a mini-boom in business investment also underpinned the currency's new found confidence.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the dollar relaxed to US$0.8108/13 from an early US$0.8136/41, but was still up on Friday's late US$0.8085/95 and far above last Monday's US$0.7910/15 close.

The currency had run as far as US$0.8150 resistance offshore before the altitude began to tell and analysts thought the barrier could cap it for a day or two while investors became accoustomed to seeing the cuyrrency at six-year highs.
It was broadly stronger on the crosses, rising to 90.90/00 yen from an early 90.67/77 and 90.10/20 late here Friday, aided by rumours of further yen/A$ dual currency samurai bonds this week.
The dollar also gained ground on the mark to 1.2274/90 from 1.2184/00 late Friday helped by developments in the ERM.
On the weekend European Finance Ministers negotiated the re-entry of the Italian lira into the Exchange Rate Mechanism of the European Monetary System at a rate of 990 lire per mark.

This not only depressed the mark against the lira but lifted confidence in the whole process of monetary union in Europe which in turn lessened the mark's attractiveness as a safe haven currency, dealers said.
All this lifted the local dollar to a five year closing high on its trade weighted index of 59.6, up from 59.4 Friday.
Domestic data provided fundamental support as the strong business investment outlook reduced the risk of a rate cut.

Private new capital expenditure (CAPEX) rose 0.9 percent in the September quarter compared to median market forecasts of a 3.0 percent fall. This was a robust result given that CAPEX had jumped 13.2 percent in Q2 and promised to make a useful contribution to Q3 GDP growth.

Investment expectations for 1996/97 also topped the most optimistic estimates with the latest survey forecast being for spending of A$42.91 billion, a 19.2 percent rise on the corresponding estimate for 1995/96.

When a five year average realisation ratio was applied to this forecast it implied a rise in nominal investment spending of 15.3 percent in 1996/97 compared with the government's forecast -- which had been thought optimistic -- of 14 percent.

"The CAPEX figures all but kill the chances of a rate cut before March next year," said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia. "For the A$, it means the blue sky of 85 cents targeted for mid-1997 looks more likely."
The uptrend would not be a straight line, he added, but dips should be seen as buying opportunities by exporters who missed the chance of taking cover at 78 cents just a few weeks ago.
The next test for the local dollar would come offshore in the shape of the crucial Bank of Japan Tankan survey of business conditions on Wednesday.

If, as some expected, it showed the Japanese recovery remained fragile, it would further confirm market assumptions that rates would stay at record lows for a while yet and safeguard the A$'s yield advantage.
There was support for the steady rate view today as the Bank of Japan conceded that more financial institutions might fail, like Hanwa Bank did last week.
